title: Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event

facts.text: Marine animal life radiated through the Ordovician, replacing the Cambrian fauna with one rich in suspension feeders and swimmers.
Global diversity rose severalfold as the phyla filled out with many new classes and lower taxa.
The rise was neither global nor instantaneous; different groups diversified at different times from the Late Cambrian to the Middle Ordovician.
Proposed drivers include rising ocean oxygen, nutrients eroded from the Taconic mountains, global cooling and a meteorite shower.
It set the marine ecological template for the rest of the Paleozoic.

title: Iapetus Ocean narrows

facts.text: The Iapetus Ocean between Gondwana, Laurentia and Baltica was over 4,000 km wide at the start of the Ordovician.
Baltica drifted toward Laurentia while island arcs and microcontinents such as Ganderia were added to Laurentia and Avalonia.
As the ocean narrowed, seafloor brachiopods and trilobites spread between continents, while ostracods and fishes stayed isolated.
Several sources say Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia had joined by the end of the Ordovician, forming Euramerica (Laurussia).
Others place the final Laurentia–Baltica collision in the Silurian, during the Caledonian orogeny.

title: Nautiloid cephalopods at their height

facts.text: Nautiloids reached their peak variety, with straight, curved and coiled shells living side by side.
They spread from shallow waters into open-ocean niches at all latitudes.
New orders such as Bisonocerida and Dissidocerida appear in the Early Ordovician, and Ascocerida early in the Middle Ordovician.

The period lasts about 43.75 million years, until the Silurian begins at 443.1 Ma.
It is named after the Ordovices, a Celtic tribe of north Wales, where its rocks were first identified.

title: Early Ordovician sea-level rise floods continents

facts.text: Sea level rose more or less continuously through the Early Ordovician, levelling off around mid-period.
Shallow seas covered much of North America, Europe and Gondwana.
The flooding of Laurentia created warm shallow waters where shelled sea life thrived.
North America's Transcontinental Arch went under water, not to reappear until the Devonian.

title: First phacopid trilobites

facts.text: The trilobite order Phacopida probably first appears in the early Ordovician; nine other trilobite orders had arisen in the Cambrian.
Trilobites with schizochroal eyes appear suddenly in the early Ordovician.
A new trilobite fauna took over from the old Cambrian one during the Ordovician radiation.

title: First starfish and brittle stars

facts.text: Echinoderm diversity rose in the Early Ordovician as new classes appeared, including starfish, brittle stars and diploporitans.
The first true starfish lived alongside brittle stars; their fossil record is sparse because starfish fall apart after death.
Paracrinoids appear in the Early Ordovician and cystoids in the Middle Ordovician.

title: First stromatoporoid sponges

facts.text: Stromatoporoids, extinct reef-building sea sponges, first appear unambiguously in the Early Ordovician (Tremadocian).
Stromatoporoid reefs grew in South China from the start of the Ordovician and spread to North America and North China by mid-period.
The first order, Labechiida, quickly spread worldwide in the Middle Ordovician, diversifying abruptly in the mid-to-late Darriwilian.

title: Ordovician plankton revolution

facts.text: Several invertebrate lineages colonized open waters, starting new food chains from the end of the Cambrian into the early Ordovician.
The first phase of the GOBE, tied to planktonic communities, ended in the late Early Ordovician.
Chitinozoans radiated explosively across the Tremadocian and later became key markers for dating rocks.
Acritarchs, mostly marine algae, peaked in diversity and disparity in the Middle Ordovician.
More plankton allowed suspension feeders on the seafloor and swimmers in the water column to multiply.

title: Reef building revives after Cambrian lull

facts.text: Reefs had been rare since the archaeocyath extinction until new reef-building corals diversified in the Ordovician.
Coral reefs emerged in the early Ordovician, including the earliest known octocorals.
By the middle Tremadocian, microbe and sponge reefs occupied deeper water, as in South Korea's Dumugol Formation.

title: Sauk Sea retreats from North America

facts.text: A marine regression ended the Sauk sequence early in the Ordovician; the Tippecanoe sequence followed later in the period.
At its peak the shallow Sauk Sea had covered most of North America.

title: Strophomenid brachiopods appear

facts.text: Strophomenida, an order of articulate brachiopods, lived from the Early Ordovician to the mid Carboniferous.
They were among the most diverse and abundant Ordovician brachiopods, but the Late Ordovician mass extinction hit them hard.
Orthid brachiopods reached their peak diversity at the same time, in Ordovician shallow-shelf seas.

title: Tumblagooda trackways: animals on land

facts.text: Trackways in Western Australia's Tumblagooda Sandstone are read by some as the earliest evidence of fully terrestrial animals.
Conodonts in overlying beds now point to an early Ordovician age, though a Silurian age was once favoured.
Because the unit is poorly dated, it cannot show whether plants, which colonized land in the mid-Ordovician, got there first.

facts.text: Morocco's Fezouata Shale preserves exceptional soft-bodied fossils from the Early Ordovician.
Over 1,500 soft-bodied specimens of 50 taxa resemble Burgess Shale-type biotas, bridging the Cambrian explosion and the GOBE.
Its fauna includes Aegirocassis, a filter-feeding arthropod over 2 m long, the largest animal of its time.
The first vertebrates with true bone, jawless fishes, appear around 485 million years ago.
Armoured jawless 'ostracoderms' rose to prominence and remained the main vertebrates until the Devonian.
Early fishes lived mainly in near-shore settings such as intertidal zones and shallow lagoons.
The oldest named thelodonts, Larolepis and Stroinolepis, are from the Late Ordovician Sandbian stage.
Some accounts put the first small armoured ostracoderms, such as the plated Laurentian group, already in the late Cambrian.

facts.text: The Early Ordovician was very hot, with sea surface temperatures comparable to the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.
One set of temperature estimates falls from 43.9 °C at 485 Ma to 37.1 °C at 470 Ma.
Carbon dioxide levels were very high at the start of the period.
The long-lasting heat shaped the biodiversification that followed in the Middle Ordovician.

title: Avalonia rifts away, opening the Rheic Ocean

facts.text: Around 480 Ma the microcontinent Avalonia, including parts of future Newfoundland, southern Britain and New England, broke free from Gondwana.
A rift grew into a mid-ocean ridge between them, opening the Rheic Ocean in the Early Ordovician.
Carolina, Armorica and other terranes on Gondwana's northern margin also broke away during the Ordovician.
As Avalonia drifted north it closed the Iapetus Ocean ahead of it and opened the Rheic behind it.
Ganderia probably separated from Gondwana near the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary.

Crinoids went through the first of their two major adaptive radiations during the Ordovician.

Several eurypterid clades already existed by the Middle Ordovician, suggesting the group arose in the Cambrian.
Laurentian megalograptids were the first truly successful eurypterids, radiating in the Late Ordovician; most groups appear in the Silurian.

facts.text: Horseshoe crabs (xiphosurans) first appear in the Early Ordovician, around 480 million years ago.
The oldest known specimens, still undescribed, come from Morocco's Fezouata Formation.
The oldest named stem-xiphosuran, Lunataspis, lived in what is now Canada about 445 Ma.

facts.text: Insects are estimated to have originated about 480 million years ago, around when land plants appeared.
The 2014 study behind this allows an origin as early as the Early Ordovician or even the Cambrian.
In this version, insects' early radiation happened no later than 479 Ma, in marine or coastal settings.
Volcanic island arcs collided with Laurentia, raising a great mountain chain from eastern Canada down the east of today's United States.
A change in plate motions in the middle Ordovician set the stage for this first Paleozoic mountain building in North America.
The orogeny affected most of New England.
Erosion of the new mountains fed iron and phosphorus to the oceans, a proposed driver of the GOBE.
Weathering of the rising Appalachians and Caledonides drew down CO2 in the Late Ordovician.

facts.text: Oxygen isotopes in conodonts show the climate began shifting from greenhouse to icehouse at the end of the Early Ordovician.
A sharp Floian rise in carbon isotope ratios may mark cooling through organic carbon burial, proposed to have kick-started the GOBE.
By the end of the Middle Ordovician, low-latitude sea surfaces had cooled to today's equatorial temperatures.
Graptolite ranges suggest Earth was in a mild icehouse state by about 460 million years ago.
Biodiversity rose in step with cooling during the GOBE.
A meteor about 200 m wide struck what is now Decorah, Iowa, around 470 million years ago.
The possible crater, about 5.6 km across and now buried under the Winneshiek Shale, formed with energy equal to 1,000 megatons of TNT.
It may be part of the Ordovician meteor event.

facts.text: Cryptospores, the spores of the first land plants, appear about 470 million years ago and dominate plant fossil assemblages for some 60 million years.
Land plants evolved from green algae; the earliest were bryophytes, similar to mosses and liverworts.
Baltica was an early cradle of land plants, with a diverse flora by the Darriwilian.
By burying organic carbon, they began drawing down CO2 and transforming land environments and the global climate.
Without deep roots, they did little to break rock into soil.

facts.text: An impact in Quebec, Canada, formed the 26 km Clearwater East crater; argon-argon dating of its impact melt gives about 460-470 Ma.
Its neighbour Clearwater West formed much later, in the Early Permian; their different meteorite signatures show adjacent craters need not be twins.
Its central peak, hidden under lake water and sediment, was confirmed by bathymetric surveys and core drilling.

facts.text: Atmospheric oxygen rose between 470 and 400 Ma, the Paleozoic Oxidation Event.
The first land plants, spreading from about 470 to 445 Ma, trapped organic carbon in sediments and reduced the oxygen sink.
Oxygen later reached and exceeded today's level of about 21% in the early Carboniferous.

facts.text: The break-up of the L-chondrite parent body in space sent fragments into Earth-crossing orbits.
About 100 times as many meteorites struck Earth each year as today, and the raised rate lasted for millions of years.
Shock ages in many L-chondrite meteorites that still fall today, and helium-3 in seafloor sediments, support the event.
Craters such as Ames (16 km, Oklahoma), Rock Elm (6 km, Wisconsin) and Slate Islands, and possibly Decorah and Granby, may belong to this shower.
It was once suggested to have sparked the GOBE, but other evidence puts it about 600,000 years after the Darriwilian diversity burst.

facts.text: Sediments filling the Decorah crater preserve conodonts, bivalved arthropods and the earliest eurypterids in exceptional detail.
A long ice age, also called the Andean-Saharan glaciation, lasted from about 460 to 420 million years ago.
Glaciers were probably present in Gondwana by the Sandbian, with several short glaciations then and in the Katian.
Ice centred on the Sahara in the Ordovician and shifted to South America in the Silurian; it is known from Arabia, West Africa and the Andes.
Gondwana's position over the South Pole may have allowed ice to form despite high CO2 levels.
Sea level rose and fell as ice caps grew and melted.

facts.text: Back-arc spreading split the Hunic terranes from Gondwana in the late Ordovician, opening the Paleo-Tethys Ocean.

facts.text: The Kazakh terranes, an equatorial archipelago of island arcs and microcontinents, merged as part of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt.
Accretion of crust to paleo-Kazakhstan was complete by the end of the Ordovician and Silurian.
Another account places the amalgamation of these Central Asian terranes into Kazakhstania in the late Silurian.

facts.text: An asteroid about 600 m across blasted the 7.5 km Lockne crater in what is now northern Sweden.
The smaller Målingen crater, 16 km away, may be its twin, made by a body about 250 m across.
Chitinozoan microfossils date the impact to about 458 million years ago.
A meteorite impact made the 4 km Kärdla crater in what is now Estonia, about 455 million years ago.
Huge eruptions during the Taconic orogeny, probably from a volcanic arc, left ash now preserved as the Deicke and Millbrig bentonites on Laurentia.
The Millbrig ash fall, about 454 Ma, was the largest in the last 590 million years.
Each eruption's ash layer was larger in volume than that of the Toba eruption.
The Guttenberg carbon isotope excursion began just above the base of the Katian Stage, dated to 452.8 million years ago.
Its base helps fix the Katian boundary at Black Knob Ridge, Oklahoma, together with the first appearance of the graptolite Diplacanthograptus caudatus.

facts.text: Global temperatures rose briefly in the early Katian, the Boda Event, building reef mounds and spreading fauna across Europe.

title: Extinction rates rise in the Katian

facts.text: Extinction rates rose significantly in the early or middle Katian, several million years before the Hirnantian glaciation.
This early phase of extinction is linked to large igneous province activity, possibly the Alborz LIP of northern Iran, and to the Boda event.
Bryozoan losses were drawn out: their extinction rates were higher in the early and late Katian, and origination rates dropped sharply in the late Katian.

facts.text: The oldest clear evidence of animals on land is of arthropods around 450 Ma.
Myriapods, arachnids and hexapods began colonizing land at least from the Ordovician.
They may have thrived on the food supply provided by early land plants.
Late Ordovician trace fossils a little over 445 Ma probably record land invertebrates.
Eastern Avalonia collided with Baltica at about 30°S, closing the Tornquist Sea.
The collision formed the north-western Trans-European Suture Zone and coincided with the Shelveian orogeny of western England and Wales.
It stopped the Rheic Ocean widening south of Avalonia, with huge magmatism in Avalonia and a gigantic ash fall in Baltica.
Avalonian magmatism peaked between 457 and 449 Ma.

facts.text: A stony meteorite struck what is now Charlevoix, Quebec, leaving a structure about 54 km across.
Its age, 450 ± 20 million years, spans the Ordovician to Silurian.
Long-lived intraplate mountain building, with north-south shortening of under 100 km, began in central Australia about 450 Ma and ended about 300 Ma.
Beginning in the Late Ordovician, its folding of central Australian basins had raised the MacDonnell Ranges by the Carboniferous.
It may have tilted the sandstone layers of Uluru to near vertical.

title: Possible Deniliquin impact in Australia

facts.text: A deeply buried multiple-ring structure at Deniliquin, south-east Australia, has been dated to around the start of the first extinction pulse.
A 2023 paper proposed that its impact winter triggered the Hirnantian glaciation and extinction; the idea remains untested.

contested_note: A single 2023 proposal, described as untested; the structure is not listed as a confirmed impact crater.

facts.text: A positive carbon isotope excursion, the HICE, ran through the Hirnantian alongside the short but large glaciation.
Its cause is still debated, but it is a key marker for defining the Ordovician–Silurian boundary worldwide.
Its exact age is uncertain because the Hirnantian is short and dating errors are comparatively large.

title: Hirnantian glaciation at its peak

facts.text: A sudden cooling at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary rapidly expanded glaciers, one of the most severe glaciations of the Phanerozoic.
Ice caps covered Gondwana over the South Pole, in today's Africa and South America; the cold was probably harsher than the Last Glacial Maximum.
Oxygen isotope ratios jumped by an extraordinary 2–4‰ at the start of the Hirnantian, and CO2 dropped sharply.
Sea level fell sharply, from about 220 m above today's to about 141 m.
The ice retreated abruptly at the end of the Hirnantian, and Earth returned to a much warmer climate in the Rhuddanian.

title: Hirnantian ocean anoxic event

facts.text: As the glaciers retreated, black shales spread from isolated basins to all latitudes and depths, marking a global anoxic event.
Repeated spells of anoxia mark the Ordovician–Silurian boundary.
Anoxia is the most common suspect for the extinction's second pulse; sudden volcanism may have supplied sulphur dioxide that favoured euxinia.
The Hirnantian–Rhuddanian anoxia may be one of the longest-lasting anoxic events in geologic time; its cause is uncertain.

title: Beecher's Trilobite Bed preserves soft parts

facts.text: A thin shale bed in Oneida County, New York, preserves trilobites such as Triarthrus eatoni with soft tissues replaced by pyrite.
It ranks among the world's best examples of near-perfect fossil preservation.
The first jawed vertebrates, which arose from among the ostracoderms, may have appeared in the Late Ordovician, about 445 Ma.
Late Ordovician scale microfossils, possibly from acanthodians ('spiny sharks'), are the earliest evidence of jawed fish.
Jawed fish became common in the Devonian, the 'Age of Fishes'.

facts.text: The first of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions struck in two pulses: at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary and in the later Hirnantian.
Estimates run from about 60% of marine genera to 85% of marine species lost; only the end-Permian extinction was larger.
The first pulse is tied to the sudden Hirnantian glaciation; the second to warming and spreading anoxia as the ice retreated.
Trilobites lost about 70% of genera and 50% of families; many brachiopods, bryozoans and corals also vanished.
Despite its severity it changed ecosystem structure little, and diversity recovered quickly in the Silurian.
